Technologies: Wazuh · Suricata · pfSense · Sysmon · Windows Server · Ubuntu · Kali Linux · Docker

A segmented security-monitoring lab combining network and endpoint telemetry. The environment uses pfSense for network segmentation, Suricata for network intrusion detection, Wazuh for centralized monitoring and Sysmon for Windows endpoint visibility.

The project also includes controlled attack simulations from Kali Linux against an internal OWASP Juice Shop instance in order to validate detection and alerting capabilities.

docs.title: Active Directory Attack & Defense Lab
docs.text:
Technologies: Active Directory · Windows Server · DNS · Kerberos · Ubuntu · DVWA · Impacket · Hashcat · GPO · Network Segmentation

An end-to-end Active Directory security lab combining offensive analysis and defensive hardening.

The attack scenario starts from an external Kali Linux machine, compromises an exposed DVWA web server through command injection, escalates privileges on Ubuntu, pivots into the internal network and abuses Kerberos and excessive Active Directory permissions through Kerberoasting, DCSync and Pass-the-Hash until obtaining NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM access on the Domain Controller.

The second phase focuses on reducing the attack surface through network segmentation, firewall rules, security zones, least privilege, service-account hardening and GPO-based security controls, while identifying relevant Blue Team detection opportunities.

View the project →

docs.title: TryHackMe: CMSpit
docs.text:
Authorized educational environment

This write-up documents cybersecurity techniques performed exclusively in an authorized TryHackMe training environment. All hosts, accounts, credentials, flags and data shown belong to isolated lab systems and are not production resources. Screenshots are retained as technical evidence of the exercise.

Difficulty: Medium Category: Web Exploitation & Privilege Escalation

docs.title: 1. Context & Objectives
docs.text: The objective of this assessment is to identify and exploit vulnerabilities within a web application environment, specifically targeting a Content Management System (CMS), and to demonstrate privilege escalation techniques using misconfigured system binaries.

docs.title: 2. Reconnaissance & Enumeration
docs.text:
The assessment began with an external port scan targeting the application server at 10.10.134.1.

nmap -sV --top-ports 1000 10.10.134.1

The scan identified an active web service on port 80. Navigating to the application (http://10.10.134.1/auth/login?to=/) revealed a login interface.

Further fingerprinting confirmed the application is running Cockpit CMS version 0.11.1.

docs.title: NoSQL Injection & Remote Code Execution (RCE)
docs.text:
Researching Cockpit CMS 0.11.1 revealed a known exploit chaining two NoSQL injection vulnerabilities to retrieve user lists and password reset tokens, ultimately leading to a command injection vulnerability (Metasploit module: exploit/multi/http/cockpit_cms_rce).

After configuring the payload (RHOSTS, LHOST), the exploit successfully enumerated 4 valid users: admin, darkStar7471, skidy, and ekoparty.

Targeting the skidy account (skidy@tryhackme.fakemail) via the /auth/resetpassword endpoint bypassed the authentication mechanism, granting an initial meterpreter shell on the target system.

Directory traversal through the established session allowed the retrieval of the initial web flag.

docs.title: Database Enumeration
docs.text:
Further exploration of the local environment identified a user named stux. Enumerating the database files revealed a hidden .dbshell configuration file in their home directory.

This file contained hardcoded credentials and a database flag.

Using the recovered password, an interactive shell session was established as the stux user to retrieve the standard user flag.

docs.title: Sudo Misconfiguration & Command Injection
docs.text:
A review of local permissions (sudo -l) revealed a critical misconfiguration: the stux user was permitted to execute the exiftool binary with root privileges without requiring a password.

The installed version of exiftool was vulnerable to CVE-2021-22204 (Command Injection). By utilizing the djvumake utility, a malicious proof-of-concept (PoC) file was crafted. When processed by exiftool via sudo, it executed the embedded payload with root privileges, successfully copying and reading the root.txt flag.

docs.title: 6. The Defender's View (Remediation)
docs.text:
To secure this environment and mitigate the identified attack paths, the following remediations must be applied:

  1. CMS Patching: Upgrade Cockpit CMS to the latest stable release to patch the NoSQL injection and command injection vulnerabilities.

  2. Secure Configuration Storage: Never store plain-text passwords or sensitive tokens in configuration or history files (e.g., .dbshell). Implement strict file permissions (600) for user-specific configuration files.

  3. Principle of Least Privilege (Sudo): Revoke the NOPASSWD sudo execution rights for the exiftool binary. Sudo privileges should only be granted for specific, required operational scripts, not interactive or parse-heavy binaries.

  4. Vulnerability Management: Update exiftool to a patched version to remediate CVE-2021-22204, preventing arbitrary code execution via crafted files.

docs.title: JBoss & JMX Console Analysis:
docs.text: JBoss (now known as WildFly) is an enterprise Java Application Server used for hosting complex applications. Further enumeration of port 8080 revealed an exposed JMX (Java Management Extensions) Console accessible at /jmx-console/. The JMX Console is a built-in management tool that allows administrators to interact with Managed Beans (MBeans). Exposing this interface without proper authentication presents a critical security risk, as it permits arbitrary administrative actions.

docs.title: 3. Exploitation (Initial Access)
docs.text:
To leverage the exposed JMX console, the jexboss framework (an automated exploitation tool designed for JBoss/Tomcat environments) was utilized.

The tool successfully exploited the misconfiguration, deploying a payload that yielded a reverse shell on the target system. This initial foothold provided unauthorized access as a standard service user, allowing for the retrieval of the initial flag.

To facilitate reliable enumeration and further exploitation, the shell was upgraded to a fully interactive session using Metasploit.

docs.title: 4. Privilege Escalation (PrivEsc)
docs.text:
With local access established, the system was audited for privilege escalation vectors. A search for files with the Set-User-ID (SUID) bit enabled was executed to identify binaries that run with root privileges.

The results highlighted a non-standard, custom binary named pingsys. Because the SUID bit was set, executing pingsys runs the application in the context of the root user rather than the current low-privileged user.

Subsequent testing of pingsys revealed that it accepts user input (such as an IP address to ping) but fails to properly sanitize it before passing it to the underlying operating system. By utilizing command injection payloads (e.g., appending commands with ; or &&), arbitrary commands were successfully executed as root.

This vulnerability allowed for complete system compromise and the retrieval of the root flag.

docs.title: 5. The Defender's View (Remediation)
docs.text:
To secure this environment and mitigate the identified attack paths, the following remediation strategies must be implemented:

  1. Secure the JMX Console: The JBoss JMX Console should never be exposed to untrusted networks. Implement strict authentication (username and password) and restrict network access to the interface using firewall rules so that only authorized administrator IPs can reach it.

  2. Patch and Update JBoss: Ensure the JBoss/WildFly application server is updated to the latest stable release to patch known remote code execution vulnerabilities and insecure default configurations.

  3. Remediate Custom SUID Binaries: Immediately remove the SUID bit from the pingsys binary (chmod u-s /path/to/pingsys). If the binary is strictly required for business operations, its source code must be rewritten to implement rigorous input validation and sanitization to prevent command injection.

  4. Principle of Least Privilege: Audit all system binaries and ensure no custom or unnecessary tools are granted elevated execution rights.

docs.title: TryHackMe: Retro
docs.text:
Authorized educational environment

This write-up documents cybersecurity techniques performed exclusively in an authorized TryHackMe training environment. All hosts, accounts, credentials, flags and data shown belong to isolated lab systems and are not production resources. Raw secret values are redacted from rendered commands where they are not necessary to understand the methodology; all attack steps and technical conclusions are preserved.

Difficulty: Hard Platform: TryHackMe Target: Windows Objective: Initial Access & Local Privilege Escalation

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
In this room, the objective is to compromise a Windows machine and ultimately obtain the highest level of local privileges.

The attack can be divided into several main phases:

  1. Enumerating the web server.
  2. Identifying the WordPress installation and valid users.
  3. Gaining access to the WordPress administration interface.
  4. Achieving remote command execution through the WordPress theme editor.
  5. Accessing the Windows desktop through RDP.
  6. Enumerating the system for possible privilege-escalation vectors.
  7. Investigating CVE-2019-1388.
  8. Exploiting CVE-2017-0213 to obtain NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges.

All actions described in this write-up were performed inside the authorized TryHackMe laboratory environment.

docs.title: 2.1. Directory Enumeration with Gobuster
docs.text:
We begin by enumerating the web server in order to discover directories that may not be directly visible from the main page.

gobuster dir -u http://10.129.189.26 \
-w /usr/share/wordlists/dirbuster/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt

Gobuster discovers several interesting directories, including:

/retro
/Retro

The /retro directory contains a website and therefore becomes our main target for further investigation.

docs.title: 2.2. WordPress Enumeration with WPScan
docs.text:
After discovering the website, we identify it as a WordPress installation.

We use WPScan to gather additional information about the WordPress environment.

WPScan is specifically designed for WordPress enumeration and can help identify information such as:

  • WordPress versions
  • Users
  • Installed themes
  • Plugins
  • Configuration information
  • Known vulnerabilities

During the enumeration, WPScan identifies a valid WordPress user:

wade

Discovering a valid username significantly reduces the authentication attack surface because we now know that wade corresponds to an existing account.

docs.title: 2.3. Inspecting the Website Source Code
docs.text:
We continue the enumeration by inspecting the HTML source code of the website.

The source contains several references to WordPress resources and to a theme named:

90s-retro

These references confirm that the website is powered by WordPress and provide additional information about its structure.

Identifying the active theme will later become particularly useful once administrative access is obtained.

docs.title: 2.4. Inspecting the WordPress REST API
docs.text:
WordPress exposes a REST API that can provide information about the website depending on its configuration.

By inspecting the available API endpoints, we observe references to WordPress REST API version 2 as well as namespaces such as:

oembed/1.0

The API provides another potential source of information during the enumeration phase.

docs.title: 2.5. Investigating CVE-2017-6514
docs.text:
During our research, we investigate CVE-2017-6514.

The vulnerability is associated with information disclosure involving WordPress user information.

From an attacker's perspective, information-disclosure vulnerabilities can be valuable because they may reveal valid usernames or other details that can later be used during authentication attempts.

docs.title: 2.6. Examining WordPress User Information
docs.text:
We inspect the WordPress API response associated with the user wade.

The returned JSON information confirms details such as:

  • User ID
  • Username
  • Author information
  • Associated URLs

Most importantly, this confirms that:

wade

is a valid WordPress account.

docs.title: 3.1. Accessing the WordPress Dashboard
docs.text:
Using the credentials recovered during our enumeration, we successfully authenticate to the WordPress administration dashboard.

Administrative access considerably increases our attack possibilities because WordPress administrators can modify files belonging to installed themes.

We navigate to:

Appearance → Theme Editor → 404 Template (404.php)

The WordPress theme editor allows us to directly modify PHP files used by the website.

Since PHP code contained inside these files is processed by the web server, modifying a theme file gives us a potential way to execute commands on the underlying Windows system.

docs.title: 3.2. Preparing Remote Access
docs.text:
Our next objective is to move from WordPress administrative access to command execution on the Windows host.

We modify the 404.php template and insert PHP code designed to interact with the operating system.

One approach is to create a reverse shell using functions such as:

fsockopen()

to establish the network connection and:

proc_open()

to start:

cmd.exe

The principle of a reverse shell is that the compromised server initiates the connection back to our Kali machine.

This avoids relying exclusively on commands executed through the browser and can provide a more interactive command-line session.

docs.title: 3.3. Confirming Remote Command Execution
docs.text:
Before relying on a reverse shell, we verify that our modified PHP file is capable of executing Windows commands.

We request the modified 404.php page while supplying the dir command:

http://10.129.189.26/retro/wp-content/themes/90s-retro/404.php?cmd=dir

The resulting page displays the output of the Windows dir command.

We can see the files contained inside the WordPress theme directory.

This confirms an important milestone:

We have successfully achieved remote command execution on the Windows server through the WordPress application.

At this point, our access is no longer limited to WordPress itself. We can interact with the underlying Windows operating system within the security context of the web-server process.

docs.title: 4.1. Connecting Through RDP
docs.text:
After obtaining valid Windows credentials, we attempt to access the graphical Windows environment using Remote Desktop Protocol.

From Kali Linux, we use FreeRDP:

xfreerdp /u:wade /p:<LAB_PASSWORD_REDACTED> /v:10.129.189.26 /dynamic-resolution +clipboard

The main parameters are:

  • /u:wade — username
  • /p:<LAB_PASSWORD_REDACTED> — recovered lab password (redacted in the rendered write-up)
  • /v:10.129.189.26 — target host
  • /dynamic-resolution — dynamically adjusts the remote desktop resolution
  • +clipboard — enables clipboard sharing between Kali and Windows

Authentication succeeds and we obtain an interactive Windows desktop session as:

Wade

We now have direct access to the target machine as a local user.

docs.title: 4.2. Retrieving the User Flag
docs.text:
Once connected through RDP, we inspect Wade's desktop.

A file named:

user.txt

is present.

Opening the file with Notepad reveals the user flag.

This confirms that we have successfully completed the initial-access portion of the room.

docs.title: 5. Privilege Escalation Enumeration
docs.text:
Although we now have access to the Windows machine, Wade is not running with the highest system privileges.

Our next objective is therefore to identify a local privilege-escalation technique that allows us to move from the current account to a privileged security context.

The ultimate goal is to obtain either Administrator-level access or, preferably:

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

SYSTEM is one of the most privileged local security contexts available on Windows.

docs.title: 5.1. Investigating CVE-2019-1388
docs.text:
One potential privilege-escalation technique we investigate is:

CVE-2019-1388

This vulnerability involves Windows certificate dialogs and certain privileged operations performed through the Windows graphical interface.

Under vulnerable configurations, interactions with certificate information may lead to the creation of a process with elevated privileges.

docs.title: 5.2. Exploring Windows User Accounts
docs.text:
As part of the local enumeration process, we navigate to:

C:\Users

Several user directories are visible, including:

Administrator
Public
Wade

This confirms that our current session belongs to the Wade account and that a separate Administrator profile exists on the machine.

docs.title: 5.3. Testing User Account Control
docs.text:
We then investigate the behavior of Windows User Account Control, commonly known as UAC.

UAC is designed to prevent applications from silently acquiring elevated privileges.

When an application requests administrative permissions, Windows may display a prompt asking the user either to confirm the action or to provide administrator credentials.

In our case, attempting to execute the application with elevated privileges results in a credential prompt.

This indicates that Wade cannot simply approve administrative execution.

docs.title: 5.4. Investigating the Certificate Dialog
docs.text:
Because CVE-2019-1388 is related to the Windows certificate interface, we inspect the certificate information presented by the executable.

The application is displayed as being published by Microsoft Windows, and Windows allows us to inspect additional certificate and publisher information.

This dialog is particularly interesting because certain historical Windows privilege-escalation techniques abused interactions originating from a privileged certificate window.

docs.title: 5.5. Testing the CVE-2019-1388 Approach
docs.text:
We continue interacting with the UAC and certificate windows in order to determine whether we can launch another process from the privileged security context.

The objective is to escape from the restricted dialog and obtain access to a privileged Windows process.

However, this approach does not provide us with a reliable privilege-escalation path in our current environment.

We therefore continue our enumeration instead of relying on this technique.

docs.title: 5.6. Investigating Internet Explorer
docs.text:
During the investigation, Internet Explorer is opened as part of the certificate-related workflow.

The browser attempts to access a certificate-related resource, but the requested page cannot be displayed.

We inspect the available browser options to determine whether Internet Explorer can be leveraged to start another process with elevated privileges.

Since this path does not provide the desired result, we move on to another local privilege-escalation vulnerability.

docs.title: 6. Privilege Escalation with CVE-2017-0213
docs.text:
We next investigate:

CVE-2017-0213

This vulnerability affects Microsoft Windows and can allow a local user to elevate privileges on a vulnerable system.

It is associated with Windows COM mechanisms and improper handling of privileged operations.

For our attack scenario, this vulnerability is particularly interesting because we already satisfy the most important prerequisite:

We already have local access to the target machine as Wade.

A successful exploitation can therefore allow us to transition from the security context of Wade to:

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

docs.title: 6.1. Obtaining the Exploit
docs.text:
We locate a public proof of concept for CVE-2017-0213 in the windows-kernel-exploits repository.

The available files contain different versions of the exploit for different system architectures.

Because the target machine is running a 64-bit version of Windows, we select the appropriate 64-bit executable.

At this stage, the exploit exists on our Kali machine.

We still need to transfer it to the target Windows machine before it can be executed.

docs.title: 6.2. Hosting the Exploit with a Python HTTP Server
docs.text:
A simple way to transfer files between our Kali attacking machine and the Windows target is to temporarily host them over HTTP.

Inside the directory containing the exploit, we start Python's built-in HTTP server.

For example:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Python starts a lightweight web server listening on port 8000.

The directory from which the command is executed becomes accessible over HTTP.

Conceptually, the situation is now:

Kali Linux
   |
   |  Python HTTP Server
   |  Port 8000
   |
   +---- CVE-2017-0213 exploit.exe
                |
                | HTTP
                v
        Windows Target

An important distinction is that the Python server itself does not exploit the Windows machine.

Its only purpose is to make the exploit executable available for download.

docs.title: 6.3. Downloading the Exploit onto Windows
docs.text:
From the Windows target, we open a browser and navigate to the IP address of our Kali machine on the port used by the Python HTTP server.

The browser displays the directory listing exposed by Python.

We can see the CVE-2017-0213 executable hosted on Kali.

This demonstrates that network communication works in the following direction:

Windows Target  ─────HTTP request─────>  Kali
Windows Target  <────exploit.exe──────  Kali

We then download the 64-bit exploit onto the Windows machine.

This step is often described as transferring a payload, although technically our Kali machine is hosting the file and the Windows target is downloading it.

After the transfer, the exploit executable is physically present on the target system and can be executed locally.

docs.title: 6.4. Executing CVE-2017-0213
docs.text:
We launch the downloaded executable from the Windows machine.

The exploit abuses the vulnerable Windows behavior targeted by CVE-2017-0213 and causes a new process to be created with elevated privileges.

A command prompt is opened.

To understand the significance of this new shell, it is important to distinguish the different Windows security contexts involved.

Before exploitation, our session runs as:

Wade

After successful exploitation, the newly created process runs as:

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

The privilege transition can therefore be represented as:

Wade
  |
  | CVE-2017-0213
  v
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

This confirms that the local privilege escalation was successful.

docs.title: 6.5. Understanding What Happened
docs.text:
The final exploitation process consists of several independent steps.

First, the exploit executable is located on our Kali Linux machine.

We then run:

python3 -m http.server 8000

This turns Kali into a temporary HTTP file server.

The Windows target connects to that HTTP server and downloads the executable.

Therefore, the Python server does not directly give us SYSTEM privileges.

Its role is only:

File Transfer

The actual privilege escalation occurs only once the downloaded CVE-2017-0213 executable is launched on the vulnerable Windows machine.

The complete attack flow is therefore:

                    ATTACKER
                  Kali Linux
                      |
                      |
             CVE-2017-0213.exe
                      |
                      v
            Python HTTP Server
                 Port 8000
                      |
                      | HTTP download
                      |
                      v
                WINDOWS TARGET
                      |
                    Wade
                      |
                      | Execute exploit
                      |
                      v
               CVE-2017-0213
                      |
                      | Privilege Escalation
                      |
                      v
           NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

In other words:

  1. We obtain the exploit on Kali.
  2. We host it using Python's HTTP server.
  3. The Windows machine connects to our Kali HTTP server.
  4. We download the exploit onto Windows.
  5. We execute the exploit locally.
  6. CVE-2017-0213 abuses a vulnerable Windows mechanism.
  7. Windows starts a new process with elevated privileges.
  8. We obtain a command prompt running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM is not simply another normal Windows user.

It is the local system account used by Windows itself and by many privileged system services.

It generally has permissions exceeding those of standard users and is one of the highest local privilege levels available on a Windows machine.

Therefore, obtaining a shell as:

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

means that the privilege-escalation phase has succeeded and that we have effectively gained full control of the target machine within the laboratory environment.

docs.title: 7. Attack Chain Summary
docs.text:
The complete compromise can be summarized as follows:

Web Server Enumeration
        |
        v
Discovery of /retro
        |
        v
WordPress Enumeration
        |
        v
Valid User: wade
        |
        v
WordPress Administrative Access
        |
        v
Theme Editor
        |
        v
PHP Command Execution
        |
        v
Remote Command Execution
        |
        v
Windows Credentials
        |
        v
RDP Access as Wade
        |
        v
Local Privilege Escalation Enumeration
        |
        +---- CVE-2019-1388 Investigation
        |
        v
CVE-2017-0213
        |
        v
Exploit Transferred Through Python HTTP Server
        |
        v
Exploit Executed Locally
        |
        v
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

docs.title: 8. Conclusion
docs.text:
The Retro room demonstrates an attack chain involving both web application compromise and Windows local privilege escalation.

We began by enumerating the web server and identifying a WordPress installation under /retro.

WordPress enumeration revealed the valid user wade, and access to the administration interface allowed us to modify a PHP theme file.

By abusing the WordPress theme editor, we confirmed remote command execution on the underlying Windows host.

Valid Windows credentials then allowed us to establish an RDP session as Wade and directly interact with the system.

During privilege-escalation enumeration, we first investigated CVE-2019-1388 and the Windows certificate dialog but ultimately moved to CVE-2017-0213.

We transferred the CVE-2017-0213 exploit from Kali to the Windows machine using a temporary Python HTTP server.

Once the executable was downloaded and executed locally, the vulnerability allowed us to elevate our privileges from the Wade account to:

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

The most important lesson from the final stage is that the Python HTTP server was only the file-transfer mechanism. The actual privilege escalation occurred when the vulnerable Windows machine executed the CVE-2017-0213 exploit.

The final compromise path was therefore:

WordPress
    ↓
Remote Command Execution
    ↓
RDP as Wade
    ↓
Local Exploit Transfer
    ↓
CVE-2017-0213
    ↓
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

This completes the compromise of the Retro machine.

docs.title: 2. Setup
docs.text:
Impacket is a collection of Python classes for working with network protocols. It is a library that developers use to build security tools, but it also comes with a suite of ready-to-use scripts.

  • What it does: It allows you to "talk" to Windows systems using low-level protocols like SMB, MSRPC, and Kerberos without needing a Windows machine.
  • Common Use: If you have a password or a hash, you use Impacket scripts (like psexec.py or wmiexec.py) to remotely execute commands on a target, dump credentials (secretsdump.py), or manipulate Kerberos tickets.

BloodHound is an analytical tool (not a library) used to reveal the hidden, often complex relationships within an Active Directory environment.

  • What it does: It uses graph theory to map out how users, groups, computers, and permissions are connected. It answers the question: "I am a regular user; what is the shortest path of permissions I need to take to become a Domain Admin?"
  • Common Use: You run a "collector" (SharpHound) on a network to gather data, then you import that data into the BloodHound GUI to visualize attack paths like "User A is a member of Group B, which has Admin rights on Computer C, where a Domain Admin is logged in."

Neo4j is a graph database management system. It is the backend database that powers BloodHound.

  • What it does: Unlike a traditional spreadsheet-style database (SQL), Neo4j stores data as "Nodes" (entities like Users or Computers) and "Edges" (relationships like MemberOf or HasSession).
  • Common Use: You don't usually interact with Neo4j directly during a pentest; instead, you start the Neo4j service so that BloodHound has a place to store and quickly query the massive web of AD connections you've collected.

docs.title: 5. Abusing Kerberos
docs.text:
What is ASREPRoasting? In a standard Kerberos login, Pre-Authentication is required. This means your computer sends a timestamp encrypted with your password hash to the Domain Controller (DC). The DC decrypts it to prove you are who you say you are before it sends you a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT).

However, if an account has the attribute "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication" (UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH) enabled:

  • You (the attacker) send a request (AS-REQ) for a ticket for that username.
  • The DC says, "Sure, I don't need proof yet," and sends back an encrypted ticket (AS-REP).
  • Part of that ticket is encrypted with the user's password hash. You can now take that "blob" of data home and use a tool like Hashcat or John the Ripper to guess the password until the math matches.

7. Elevating privileges within the domain
docs.text:
What is DCSync? DCSync is a technique that mimics the behavior of a Domain Controller (DC). In a healthy Active Directory environment, DCs need to stay in sync with each other. They do this by "replicating" data—sharing updates about users, groups, and, most importantly, password hashes.

An account like backup (in this lab) has been granted specific Replication Permissions. Because it has these rights, it can tell the main Domain Controller: "Hey, I'm a fellow DC. Please sync your database with me."

The Domain Controller, believing the request is legitimate, sends over the requested objects, including the NTLM hashes of every single user in the domain.

DRSUAPI stands for the Directory Replication Service Remote Protocol. It is the specific "language" that Windows Domain Controllers use to communicate with each other to keep their databases in sync. When you hear "DCSync," you are essentially hearing about the exploitation of this protocol.

docs.text: Pass-the-Hash (PtH) is a technique where you authenticate to a remote server using a captured NTLM hash instead of the plaintext password. It works because the NTLM protocol uses the hash itself as the "secret" during the challenge-response handshake, so the server never needs to see the original password. This allows you to bypass the cracking phase entirely and gain immediate access to systems.

Hybrid SOC — Network and Endpoint Threat Detection
docs.text:
pfSense · Suricata · Wazuh · Windows Server / Sysmon · Ubuntu · Docker / OWASP Juice Shop · Kali Linux

Project status — evolving documentation

This SOC laboratory is under active evaluation and continuous improvement. The documentation captures the current architecture, available evidence, detection logic and reproducible security exercises; it is not a frozen final release. Test coverage, investigation records and supporting screenshots are updated as the laboratory evolves.

A virtualized cybersecurity laboratory combining perimeter monitoring, endpoint telemetry, centralized event analysis, detection engineering and structured incident investigation. The environment separates an external attacker segment from a protected internal network and uses deliberately vulnerable web infrastructure for controlled security validation.

SOC workflow: network segmentation → traffic inspection → host monitoring → log collection → rule-based classification → analyst triage → controlled response → detection-quality assessment.

Scope: All IP addresses belong to a private virtual laboratory. Attack examples target only owned or explicitly authorized lab resources.

docs.title: 1. Context and business objectives
docs.text:
Modern SOC teams do more than install intrusion detection software: they must collect usable telemetry from heterogeneous assets, recognize meaningful threats, reconstruct the events surrounding an alert and select responses appropriate to the risk. This project models that workflow in a compact virtual enterprise environment.

The engineering scope covers:

  • creating a clear trust boundary between an untrusted network and protected internal systems;
  • exposing only the required application service through a controlled NAT rule;
  • deploying a network intrusion detection sensor where inbound traffic becomes visible;
  • using a central SIEM to organize endpoint and network security events;
  • making endpoint telemetry actionable with Sysmon, Windows Security events, Linux logs and file integrity monitoring;
  • defining version-controlled detection logic and benign/malicious test cases;
  • formalizing analyst investigations and safe response mechanisms.

The project emphasizes detection evidence, data-source quality, false-positive analysis and reproducibility, rather than equating a vulnerability probe with successful exploitation.

pfSense: ingress filtering, NAT, management-plane access control and perimeter log production.

Suricata: packet inspection and Emerging Threats Open signature matching on the LAN-side interface. Its role here is NIDS: the captured configuration has blocking disabled.

Wazuh: endpoint agent management, log decoding, rules, alert handling, search and investigation. The all-in-one deployment uses Wazuh Manager, Wazuh Indexer and Wazuh Dashboard; a separate Elasticsearch cluster is not implied.

Sysmon / Windows events: richer endpoint process metadata, registry/file/network activity where enabled by the selected configuration, authentication and PowerShell auditing.

docs.text:
The VMware configuration separates the test traffic source from the internal machines. pfSense has two assigned NICs:

  • em0 (WAN): 192.168.50.254/24 on VMnet1;
  • em1 (LAN): 10.0.0.254/24 on VMnet2.

As RFC1918 traffic is intentionally used on the simulated WAN, the WAN setting that blocks private source networks is adjusted for this isolated experiment. Such an exception must not be generalized to a real Internet-connected firewall.

Validation tools for this boundary include ip route, ping, traceroute/tracepath, tcpdump and the pfSense Diagnostics/Firewall Logs screens. Policy verification distinguishes permitted web traffic from denied management and non-published ports.

docs.title: 3.2. Web application target
docs.text:
An Ubuntu server at 10.0.0.30 runs the deliberately vulnerable OWASP Juice Shop application in Docker. The host publishes container port 3000 on TCP port 80:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install docker.io -y
sudo systemctl enable --now docker
sudo docker run -d -p 80:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop
sudo docker ps

These are the container deployment commands used in the lab record. Docker may assign an autogenerated container name; use the container ID displayed by docker ps for subsequent inspections. Keep the published ports consistent with the NAT path.

Figure 3 — Running Juice Shop container, with host port 80 mapped to container port 3000.

docs.title: 3.3. Wazuh server
docs.text:
The centralized monitoring node operates at 10.0.0.10 within the internal network. Its functional components are:

  1. Wazuh Manager: registration, rule evaluation, alert creation and response integration;
  2. Wazuh Indexer: searchable event storage;
  3. Wazuh Dashboard: agent inventory, hunting, visualization and alert investigation.

Wazuh agents report to the manager using the agent protocol (commonly TCP/1514). Enrollment-related ports, certificates and firewall access are administered separately. An online agent confirms connectivity; it does not, by itself, prove that any particular event channel has been ingested.

docs.title: 3.4. Ubuntu agent enrollment
docs.text:
The Ubuntu endpoint at 10.0.0.30 has a Wazuh agent. The initial enrollment was complicated by a network change from a dynamically assigned address to the isolated static internal subnet. A duplicate-agent-name condition was identified from /var/ossec/logs/ossec.log. Clearing the stale manager-side record and re-enrolling the endpoint restored connection.

Figure 4 — Linux endpoint registered and active in Wazuh.

docs.title: 3.5. Windows Server and Sysmon
docs.text:
A Windows Server 2025 virtual machine at 10.0.0.20 supplements the Linux host. The Wazuh Windows agent is installed, and Sysmon is included in the endpoint monitoring design. The endpoint telemetry configuration targets the Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational channel.

The reported agent-version compatibility issue was resolved by aligning the Windows agent with the manager version (the screenshot displays Wazuh agent v4.9.2). This version information should be interpreted as the agent version on the endpoint inventory, not a blanket assertion about every installed component.

Figure 5 — Two active Wazuh agents: Ubuntu 10.0.0.30 and Windows Server 10.0.0.20.

docs.title: 3.6. Network intrusion detection with Suricata
docs.text:
Suricata is installed as a pfSense package and runs on the LAN interface (em1). The sensor inspects network traffic entering the protected network, using Emerging Threats Open signatures for network- and application-layer matching.

Figure 6 — Suricata active on LAN with Blocking Mode: DISABLED; detection mode, not prevention mode.

docs.title: 4.1. External attack origin
docs.text: Kali Linux at 192.168.50.100 represents the untrusted source. The separation from 10.0.0.0/24 ensures inbound application requests cross the pfSense perimeter rather than originating from the target subnet.

docs.title: 4.2. Service publication with destination NAT
docs.text:
pfSense publishes HTTP on the WAN interface and forwards it to the internal application:

NAT field Setting Interface WAN Protocol TCP External destination WAN address: 192.168.50.254 External destination port 80 Translated address 10.0.0.30 Translated port 80

Figure 7 — Port forwarding from WAN TCP/80 to Ubuntu TCP/80.

The client uses http://192.168.50.254/; pfSense translates the destination before delivering the request to the Linux host. The Docker publishing rule then directs host TCP/80 to the application on container TCP/3000.

Figure 8 — Juice Shop reached from Kali through the firewall NAT path.

docs.title: 4.3. Nmap NSE and Suricata alert analysis
docs.text:
A controlled HTTP reconnaissance/vulnerability probe from the Kali segment produced local Suricata alerts on 29 September 2026 at approximately 22:02:18 (time as displayed by pfSense).

Figure 9 — Suricata alert table for traffic from 192.168.50.100 to 10.0.0.30:80.

Field Observation from screenshot Source 192.168.50.100 (Kali) Destination 10.0.0.30:80 (Ubuntu web target) Transport TCP Example source ports 43730, 43714, 43712 Signature 1:2009358 ET SCAN Nmap Scripting Engine User-Agent Detected Signature 1:2018056 ET WEB_SERVER Possible XXE SYSTEM ENTITY in POST BODY Priority shown 1 Suricata operating mode IDS, no packet-blocking mode

Security interpretation. The sensor matched patterns associated with Nmap Scripting Engine user-agent activity and possible XXE-formatted HTTP payloads. This is evidence of suspicious traffic and correct local signature matching. It is not evidence that an XML parser resolved external entities, that data were exfiltrated, or that a Trojan executed. The same request can match more than one rule; the number of alert lines must not be interpreted as the number of distinct intrusions.

This case provides a concrete baseline for the analysis methods described below.

docs.title: 5. Centralized network telemetry — Suricata and Wazuh
5.1. Collection architecture
docs.text:
The original Nmap exercise established that Suricata can identify suspicious HTTP patterns at the LAN boundary (Figure 9). To extend that visibility beyond the firewall console, the SOC architecture uses a dedicated ingestion path for Suricata's structured EVE JSON output. This design preserves the network attributes required for investigation: source and destination IPs, translated application port, signature ID, timestamp and flow metadata.

Kali:192.168.50.100 -- HTTP --> pfSense WAN:192.168.50.254
                                       |
                                 DNAT TCP/80
                                       v
                                Ubuntu:10.0.0.30:80
                                       ^
                           Suricata NIDS (pfSense LAN)
                                       |
                                eve.json (JSONL)
                                       |
                            syslog-ng / TCP 5514
                                       |
                          rsyslog (Wazuh:10.0.0.10)
                                       |
                        /var/log/soc/suricata-eve.json
                                       |
                       Wazuh JSON collection and rules
                                       |
                         Wazuh dashboard / investigation

This pipeline is separate from pfSense firewall Syslog. Firewall filterlog entries explain whether the firewall accepted or rejected a packet; EVE alert records explain which Suricata signature matched. Both sources are useful, but they are not interchangeable. The example transport is restricted to the internal lab subnet; production-grade transport would require encryption and authentication.

docs.title: 5.2. EVE event structure and sensor configuration
docs.text:
The Suricata LAN instance is the relevant sensor because pfSense performs destination NAT before forwarding the HTTP requests to 10.0.0.30. EVE output uses one JSON object per line. Alert and HTTP metadata are the event types used for web activity correlation. The network signature in Figure 9 maps to the following significant EVE fields:

{
  "event_type": "alert",
  "src_ip": "192.168.50.100",
  "dest_ip": "10.0.0.30",
  "dest_port": 80,
  "proto": "TCP",
  "alert": {
    "signature_id": 2009358,
    "signature": "ET SCAN Nmap Scripting Engine User-Agent Detected"
  }
}

Field illustration based on the observed Suricata signature, not a verbatim capture of the native EVE file. A complete EVE record also contains event timestamps, flow identifiers and additional fields, according to the enabled output options.

The physical output path is resolved from the pfSense Suricata installation rather than hardcoded. The operational diagnostic is:

find /var/log/suricata -type f -name eve.json -print
tail -n 2 /var/log/suricata/<LAN_INSTANCE>/eve.json

<LAN_INSTANCE> denotes the actual package-generated directory for the monitored LAN interface.

docs.title: 5.3. Transfer and parsing configuration
docs.text:
The forwarding side uses syslog-ng on pfSense. Its file source reads the EVE file without parsing the line as traditional Syslog; the TCP destination sends the raw JSON line to the Wazuh host. This preserves Wazuh's native JSON decoder input.

pfSense — syslog-ng source and destination:

source s_soc_eve {
    file("/var/log/suricata/<LAN_INSTANCE>/eve.json"
         flags(no-parse) follow-freq(1));
};

destination d_soc_wazuh {
    network("10.0.0.10" transport("tcp") port(5514)
            template("${MESSAGE}\n"));
};

log {
    source(s_soc_eve);
    destination(d_soc_wazuh);
};

The corresponding repository artifact is pfsense-suricata-syslog-ng.conf. The receiver accepts only messages from the pfSense LAN IP and writes them as newline-delimited JSON.

Wazuh host — /etc/rsyslog.d/30-suricata-eve.conf:

module(load="imtcp")
template(name="SocEveJson" type="string" string="%msg%\n")
ruleset(name="soc_eve_ingress") {
    if ($fromhost-ip != "10.0.0.254") then { stop }
    action(type="omfile" file="/var/log/soc/suricata-eve.json"
           template="SocEveJson" fileCreateMode="0640"
           dirCreateMode="0750" createDirs="on")
    stop
}
input(type="imtcp" address="10.0.0.10" port="5514" ruleset="soc_eve_ingress")

The receiver definition is also stored as 30-suricata-eve.conf. The Wazuh Manager reads the preserved JSON file via the following element in its existing /var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf:

<localfile>
  <log_format>json</log_format>
  <location>/var/log/soc/suricata-eve.json</location>
</localfile>

The Wazuh built-in rule 86601 provides the starting point for Suricata alert classification. The network detection rules in Section 6 specialize this base classification without changing the original EVE record.

docs.title: 5.4. End-to-end verification and analyst fields
docs.text:
The collection chain has multiple independent points of inspection; this separation helps locate a transport or decoding problem without attributing it to a failed detection rule.

Layer Evidence source Significant control Sensor pfSense eve.json Valid JSON line with event_type=alert and signature ID Transport syslog-ng service logs; receiver 5514/TCP Single JSON record preserved per line Collection /var/log/soc/suricata-eve.json Accessible to the Wazuh log collector; no Syslog prefix Detection Wazuh alerts.json / Threat Hunting Decoder fields and parent rule 86601 Investigation Source EVE + Wazuh event Same signature, source, target, flow and normalized time

Compact verification commands on the Wazuh host:

sudo rsyslogd -N1
sudo ss -lntp | grep ':5514'
sudo tail -n 3 /var/log/soc/suricata-eve.json | jq -c .
sudo /var/ossec/bin/wazuh-analysisd -t
sudo jq -c 'select(.rule.id == "86601") | {time:.timestamp, rule:.rule.id, data:.data}' \
  /var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts.json | tail -n 5

The receiving configuration must be merged with any existing imtcp module declaration rather than loading the module twice. File ownership and JSON line formatting are material to successful ingestion. Visibility in Wazuh confirms a decoded security event; it does not independently establish successful exploitation of the target.

docs.title: 6.1. Design principles
docs.text:
The detection layer distinguishes between raw events and security decisions. A Suricata signature, Sysmon process creation, Windows failed logon or Linux integrity alert is first collected by its source. Wazuh rules then classify the event according to explicit criteria. The custom rules are maintained in a version-controlled XML file: local_rules.xml.

The Wazuh Manager's installed path is /var/ossec/etc/rules/local_rules.xml. The custom IDs 100110, 100111, 100120, 100121 and 100130 identify distinct conditions. They are not interchangeable with the original vendor rule IDs.

Detection Source Condition Custom rule Priority NET-01 Suricata EVE Nmap NSE signature ID 2009358 100110 9 NET-02 Suricata EVE Possible XXE-pattern SID 2018056 100111 10 WIN-01 Sysmon Event ID 1 PowerShell image + encoded-command switch 100120 10 WIN-02 Windows Security Event ID 4625 Failed Windows authentication 100121 5 LNX-01 Wazuh FIM Modification beneath /opt/soc-canary/ 100130 7

docs.title: 6.2. Network detection: Nmap and suspicious HTTP payloads
docs.text:
Two rules refine the native Suricata alert 86601 by matching the numeric Emerging Threats signature ID. Numeric matching prevents an alert from being missed solely because a signature description changes.

<group name="soc_lab,">
  <rule id="100110" level="9">
    <if_sid>86601</if_sid>
    <field name="alert.signature_id" type="pcre2">^2009358$</field>
    <description>SOC-LAB: Nmap scripting engine detected against monitored HTTP service</description>
    <group>soc_lab,web_recon,</group>
  </rule>

  <rule id="100111" level="10">
    <if_sid>86601</if_sid>
    <field name="alert.signature_id" type="pcre2">^2018056$</field>
    <description>SOC-LAB: HTTP payload matching a possible XXE signature</description>
    <group>soc_lab,web_probe,</group>
  </rule>
</group>

NET-02 deliberately says possible XXE pattern. A request signature alone cannot establish that an application parsed an external entity or exposed information. The original packet/HTTP response would be required for a stronger conclusion.

docs.title: 6.3. Windows detection: encoded PowerShell execution
docs.text:
WIN-01 correlates four fields from Sysmon process creation: the originating Windows event channel, event ID, executable image, and launch arguments. Its objective is to identify the encoded-command execution pattern, not the specific contents of a test script.

<rule id="100120" level="10">
  <field name="win.system.channel" type="pcre2">^Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational$</field>
  <field name="win.system.eventID" type="pcre2">^1$</field>
  <field name="win.eventdata.image" type="pcre2">(?i)\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$</field>
  <field name="win.eventdata.commandLine" type="pcre2">(?i)\s-(?:enc|encodedcommand)\b</field>
  <description>SOC-LAB: PowerShell launched with encoded-command switch (Sysmon ID 1)</description>
  <group>soc_lab,windows,powershell,</group>
</rule>

The expression covers powershell.exe and pwsh.exe, case-insensitively, when invoked with -enc or -EncodedCommand. Administrators and deployment tools can also use this switch, so detection means review required, not automatic compromise attribution.

docs.title: 6.4. Windows authentication and Linux integrity changes
docs.text:
WIN-02 highlights a Windows Security 4625 failure. It is intentionally a single-event classifier, not a brute-force threshold detector.

<rule id="100121" level="5">
  <field name="win.system.channel" type="pcre2">^Security$</field>
  <field name="win.system.eventID" type="pcre2">^4625$</field>
  <description>SOC-LAB: Failed Windows authentication (Security 4625)</description>
  <group>soc_lab,windows,authentication_failed,</group>
</rule>

LNX-01 increases the specificity of Wazuh's native file modification alert 550 for the monitored lab directory. Native events 554 (file added) and 553 (file deleted) remain distinct and are not mislabeled as modifications.

<rule id="100130" level="7">
  <if_sid>550</if_sid>
  <field name="file" type="pcre2">^/opt/soc-canary/</field>
  <description>SOC-LAB: Integrity change in the monitored Ubuntu canary directory</description>
  <group>soc_lab,linux,fim,</group>
</rule>

In dashboard documents the FIM path is commonly represented by syscheck.path; the native FIM rule matcher exposes the file field to XML conditions. This difference between rule-engine fields and indexed fields matters when diagnosing a rule.

docs.title: 6.5. Ruleset validation method
docs.text:
The complete rule file is merged into the installed Wazuh custom rules, without replacing built-in vendor files or duplicating XML root groups. Structural validation and behavior validation are independent checks:

sudo /var/ossec/bin/wazuh-analysisd -t
sudo /var/ossec/bin/wazuh-logtest

The first checks whether the manager can load its rules and configuration. The second evaluates input records through pre-decoding, decoding and rule matching. The repository includes controlled test inputs that document positive/negative patterns; they are synthetic test fixtures, not captured production alerts.

Rule Positive test Negative control 100110 Suricata SID 2009358 Unrelated Suricata SID 100120 Sysmon process with -EncodedCommand Ordinary PowerShell command without the switch 100121 Security event 4625 Successful authentication event 4624 100130 Modification below /opt/soc-canary/ Change outside the monitored directory

docs.title: 7.1. Windows Server: process and authentication visibility
docs.text:
The monitored Windows Server (10.0.0.20) combines Sysmon process creation (Event ID 1), Windows Security logon failures (Event ID 4625) and optional PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104). These sources address different questions: Sysmon identifies which executable was launched and its command line; Security events describe authentication outcomes; PowerShell logging can supply additional script context.

The Wazuh Windows agent consumes these event channels through the existing ossec.conf configuration:

<localfile>
  <location>Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational</location>
  <log_format>eventchannel</log_format>
</localfile>
<localfile>
  <location>Security</location>
  <log_format>eventchannel</log_format>
</localfile>
<localfile>
  <location>Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational</location>
  <log_format>eventchannel</log_format>
</localfile>

The Sysmon configuration must include the required process events; installation alone is not sufficient. Windows auditing also needs failed-logon collection. The local event sources are inspected with:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'; Id=1
} -MaxEvents 5

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName='Security'; Id=4625
} -MaxEvents 5

# Enable failed-logon auditing on an English-language Windows installation:
auditpol /set /subcategory:"Logon" /failure:enable

The audit subcategory may have a localized name. Event field availability depends on the login type and operating-system configuration, especially for source IP addresses.

docs.title: 7.2. Ubuntu: integrity and authentication
docs.text:
The Ubuntu web target (10.0.0.30) supplies two independent forms of evidence: Wazuh File Integrity Monitoring and OpenSSH authentication records. A dedicated /opt/soc-canary directory confines integrity experiments to a nonproduction path.

<!-- Add within the agent's existing syscheck block. -->
<directories check_all="yes" realtime="yes">/opt/soc-canary</directories>

A FIM record can establish that a monitored file was created, modified or deleted, and can include timestamps and hashes. Basic realtime FIM does not reliably identify the actor behind the change; process attribution requires additional audit instrumentation.

OpenSSH failed-authentication messages are obtained from systemd-journald or /var/log/auth.log, according to the installed Ubuntu release. For systems that use auth.log, the Wazuh agent reads the file using:

<localfile>
  <log_format>syslog</log_format>
  <location>/var/log/auth.log</location>
</localfile>

For journal-only installations, a supported journal collection configuration is needed instead. The repeated-failure detection and Active Response described in Sections 8–9 depend on real sshd records with a usable source IP.

docs.title: 8. Controlled security exercises and detection analysis
docs.text: The simulations cover both network traffic and host telemetry. Each exercise specifies where the activity originates, which component records it, which rule evaluates it, and how its significance should be interpreted. This makes the scenarios reproducible without confusing a detector's signal with exploitation or compromise.

docs.title: 8.1. SOC-01 — HTTP reconnaissance and suspicious requests
docs.text:
Activity. Kali Linux (192.168.50.100) probes the published application endpoint 192.168.50.254:80. pfSense translates traffic to 10.0.0.30:80, where the LAN-side Suricata sensor inspects it.

# Executed only from the Kali VM against the private laboratory firewall.
sudo nmap -sV -p 80 --script http-enum,http-vuln* 192.168.50.254

Network finding. Figure 9 documents the real Suricata match for Nmap NSE (2009358) and possible XXE-pattern (2018056) traffic. The same events are represented by the EVE schema and handled by Wazuh's Suricata rule 86601, with custom classifiers 100110 and 100111 for those signatures.

Investigation. The analyst links the client IP and ephemeral port to the published HTTP service, checks the flow timestamp and signature ID, then inspects HTTP response details when available. The alert supports the conclusion web reconnaissance/probing was observed; it does not justify claiming an XXE exploitation success.

Key evidence fields: src_ip, src_port, dest_ip, dest_port, alert.signature_id, flow_id, Wazuh rule.id.

docs.title: 8.2. SOC-02 — Encoded PowerShell process creation
docs.text:
Activity. A harmless payload is executed on Windows Server (10.0.0.20) using PowerShell's UTF-16LE encoded-command option. A normal PowerShell invocation provides the negative control.

$payload = "Write-Output 'SOC-LAB-ENCODED-TEST'"
$encoded = [Convert]::ToBase64String(
    [Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($payload)
)
powershell.exe -NoProfile -EncodedCommand $encoded

# Benign control with no encoded-command switch:
powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command "Write-Output 'SOC-LAB-BENIGN'"

Detection chain. Sysmon Event ID 1 → Wazuh Windows event-channel collection → custom rule 100120. The rule correlates the process image with its launch arguments rather than searching for the lab marker string.

SOC analysis. The fields win.eventdata.image, win.eventdata.commandLine, win.eventdata.parentImage, win.eventdata.user and win.eventdata.processGuid reveal the launch context. The encoded marker decodes to a benign string; therefore the alert represents a controlled behavioral detection, not a confirmed malicious execution. A production analyst would inspect the parent process and surrounding endpoint events before escalating.

docs.title: 8.3. SOC-03 — Ubuntu file integrity change
docs.text:
Activity. A lab configuration file is created, modified and removed in /opt/soc-canary, the FIM-protected directory of 10.0.0.30.

sudo install -d -m 0755 /opt/soc-canary
printf 'version=1\n' | sudo tee /opt/soc-canary/app.conf
sleep 5
printf 'version=2\n' | sudo tee /opt/soc-canary/app.conf
sleep 5
sudo rm /opt/soc-canary/app.conf

Detection chain. Wazuh FIM emits distinct native events for addition (554), modification (550) and deletion (553); the custom rule 100130 singles out modifications within the protected canary directory.

SOC analysis. The alert supplies the changed path, event type, time and relevant integrity attributes. It is evidence of file modification only. Without process-aware auditing it cannot identify who or what initiated the change, and it cannot classify the modification as malicious on its own.

docs.title: 8.4. SOC-04 — Repeated SSH failures and source-IP containment
docs.text:
Activity and perimeter path. The Ubuntu host's OpenSSH service is tested from Kali through a dedicated pfSense NAT mapping. The additional publication is strictly scoped to the lab attack source:

pfSense rule Configuration WAN destination 192.168.50.254:2222/TCP Allowed source 192.168.50.100/32 NAT target 10.0.0.30:22/TCP Protected endpoint Ubuntu Wazuh agent + OpenSSH

The exercise uses a non-privileged account soc-lab-test and a small list of deliberately invalid passwords. The administrator retains out-of-band VM-console access so a temporary source block cannot eliminate management access.

# Kali VM; the target is the user's isolated, authorized lab.
for n in $(seq 1 20); do printf 'soc-invalid-%02d\n' "$n"; done \
  > /tmp/soc-invalid-passwords.txt
hydra -l soc-lab-test -P /tmp/soc-invalid-passwords.txt \
  -s 2222 -t 2 192.168.50.254 ssh

Detection chain. Ubuntu sshd authentication events → Wazuh built-in SSH correlation rule 5763 → firewall-drop Active Response on the Ubuntu agent for 180 seconds. This is endpoint-level containment; it does not enable Suricata IPS or insert a pfSense block rule.

SOC analysis. The alert must contain a trustworthy source address. An effective response is established by three separate observations: the correlated SSH alert in Wazuh, the source-IP drop inserted in the Ubuntu firewall, and the subsequent removal of the rule after timeout. A failed connection alone cannot distinguish a Wazuh block from a routing or firewall configuration error.

docs.title: 8.5. SOC-05 — Windows failed authentication
docs.text:
Activity. An incorrect password is supplied for a dedicated Windows test identity (local user on a member server; domain identity on a domain controller).

# Standalone/member server with a pre-created local test account:
runas /user:.\soc-lab-test cmd.exe
# Enter an intentionally incorrect password at the prompt.

Detection chain. Windows Security Event ID 4625 → Wazuh Windows event channel → custom classification 100121. The investigator examines TargetUserName, LogonType, authentication status and workstation/source details where provided.

SOC analysis. An isolated error is an authentication failure, not proof of password spraying or brute force. Counts over time, distinct users and validated network source addresses are needed to classify a larger campaign. For local runas failures, the event may not include a useful remote IP.

docs.title: 8.6. SOC-06 — Network access-control verification
docs.text:
Activity. From Kali, the published HTTP port is compared with an otherwise unpublished port on the pfSense WAN address.

nc -vz -w 3 192.168.50.254 80
nc -vz -w 3 192.168.50.254 8443

Analysis. The pfSense NAT and firewall policy explain the exposure decision. A successful connection to TCP/80 is consistent with the documented Juice Shop publishing rule. The result for TCP/8443 must be compared with pfSense firewall logs to distinguish policy denial from lack of a listening service or a generic network failure. Unlike the network signature scenarios, this is principally a perimeter policy test.

docs.title: 9.1. Detection and containment are separate functions
docs.text:
The pfSense sensor in Figure 6 operates as an IDS with blocking disabled. Automated containment is therefore implemented independently through Wazuh: the manager evaluates host-based evidence and invokes an agent-side command on the endpoint that produced the relevant alert.

For the SSH scenario, the chosen condition is repeated failures matched by rule 5763, rather than a single authentication error. The destination of the Active Response is the Ubuntu machine (10.0.0.30), not pfSense.

Kali -- SSH:2222 --> pfSense NAT --> Ubuntu sshd
                                          |
                                     auth failures
                                          v
                                    Wazuh manager
                                     rule 5763
                                          |
                               Active Response command
                                          v
                               Ubuntu: firewall-drop
                               temporary IP block 180s

docs.title: 9.2. Manager configuration and execution scope
docs.text:
The response configuration belongs within the manager's existing /var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf. The shipped firewall-drop command is used when available; duplicate <command> declarations must be avoided. The relevant scope is:

<active-response>
  <disabled>no</disabled>
  <command>firewall-drop</command>
  <location>local</location>
  <rules_id>5763</rules_id>
  <timeout>180</timeout>
</active-response>

Where a command entry does not already exist, the compatible definition is:

<command>
  <name>firewall-drop</name>
  <executable>firewall-drop</executable>
  <timeout_allowed>yes</timeout_allowed>
</command>
Configuration Operational meaning rules_id=5763 Trigger after a repeated-SSH-failure detection location=local Run on the event-producing Ubuntu agent command=firewall-drop Use the Wazuh IP-drop script with the agent's host firewall timeout=180 Request a temporary block lasting 180 seconds

The endpoint requires the appropriate firewall utility and a source address extracted from the authentication event. Changing rules or manager configuration requires manager validation and a service reload; the response does not execute directly from a Markdown or XML repository file.

docs.title: 9.3. Effectiveness, safeguards and rollback
docs.text:
Verification centers on the same source IP (192.168.50.100) at three observation points: Wazuh rule.id:5763, /var/ossec/logs/active-responses.log on Ubuntu, and the Ubuntu host firewall. Connectivity through 192.168.50.254:2222 is compared before, during and after the configured interval.

# Ubuntu: inspect response activity and host firewall state.
sudo tail -n 30 /var/ossec/logs/active-responses.log
sudo iptables -S INPUT | grep '192.168.50.100' || true

# Kali: check the published SSH port during the response interval.
nc -vz -w 3 192.168.50.254 2222

A rule insertion without demonstrable connection denial, or a connection denial without a corresponding rule/action log, is not enough to attribute the result to Active Response. The host should regain the intended reachability after the timeout. An emergency rollback removes only the verified source-specific rule, not every iptables rule:

# Only for the exact matching INPUT rule, after inspecting 'iptables -S':
sudo iptables -D INPUT -s 192.168.50.100 -j DROP

The control must be limited to the attack-source subnet. Shared NAT addresses, legitimate authentication mistakes and absent source-IP fields are relevant false-positive and safety concerns. The management console remains accessible independently of SSH while source-IP blocking is exercised.

docs.title: 10.1. Investigation method
docs.text:
Each alert is evaluated through a consistent sequence: source verification → affected asset → event timeline → decoding/rule logic → corroborating telemetry → impact assessment → response decision. This makes a defensible distinction between a suspicious indicator, a verified attempt, and a confirmed security impact.

The case record retains the event timestamp, raw log and alert ID, sensor/endpoint, source and destination addresses, analyst interpretation, and any containment evidence. Time-zone normalization is essential because pfSense, Windows and Linux may display different offsets.

docs.title: 10.2. CASE-SOC-001 — Web reconnaissance at the published perimeter
docs.text:
This investigation is supported by the original NAT, application-access and Suricata screenshots (Figures 7–9).

Item Observed interpretation Test origin Kali 192.168.50.100 Published service pfSense WAN 192.168.50.254:80 Translated target Ubuntu 10.0.0.30:80 Suricata signature 2009358 — Nmap Scripting Engine User-Agent Detected Additional signature 2018056 — Possible XXE SYSTEM ENTITY in POST BODY Operating mode Suricata IDS; blocking disabled Supported finding HTTP reconnaissance/probe traffic matched local IDS signatures Not established by the evidence Successful XXE exploitation, data exfiltration or host compromise

The association between the translated backend and the original source requires the pfSense NAT context. Multiple IDS signatures may refer to the same request or flow and therefore cannot automatically be counted as independent attack attempts.

docs.title: 10.3. CASE-SOC-002 — Encoded-command PowerShell investigation model
docs.text:
A Sysmon process-creation event is examined together with its parent process, full command line, user identity and process GUID. The specific laboratory payload in Section 8.2 is intentionally harmless; its purpose is to differentiate a behavioral detection from a maliciousness verdict. Rule 100120 highlights the pattern; interpretation relies on surrounding events and the known execution context.

Investigation dimension Evidence Process identification Sysmon ID 1, Image, ProcessGuid Execution context CommandLine, ParentImage, User PowerShell context Decoded UTF-16LE argument and optional Script Block Logging Decision Authorized test vs. unexplained administrative execution vs. suspicious behavior

docs.title: 10.4. CASE-SOC-003 — SSH failures and temporary host containment model
docs.text: The relevant evidence set combines the sshd records, Wazuh 5763 alert, Active Response log, inserted host firewall rule and post-timeout connectivity state. Each element answers a different question: was there a repeated source-specific authentication pattern; did Wazuh issue an action; did Ubuntu apply the intended rule; and was it removed? The response cannot be declared effective from a single dashboard alert.

docs.title: 10.5. Incident report structure
docs.text: Record Analyst content Case ID CASE-SOC-### and detection source Time range Start/end and normalized time zone Assets Hostname, agent, source/destination and port Evidence Raw alert, rule ID, native log, screen or trace file Analysis Detection reasoning, benign alternatives, incident scope Outcome Authorized test / benign / suspicious / inconclusive Action Action owner, host, scope, timeout and rollback Improvement Rule tuning, source coverage, false-positive suppression

docs.title: 11.1. Validation criteria
docs.text:
The SOC is assessed by whether the same event can be followed from its source to an analyst decision. A dashboard alert count alone is not a performance metric. Each detection has a matching criterion and a benign control to expose overly broad rules.

Control Key data source Rule(s) Evidence to compare HTTP reconnaissance Suricata EVE 86601, 100110, 100111 Signature ID, network tuple and event time Encoded PowerShell Sysmon ID 1 100120 Image + command line; normal PowerShell negative control Windows authentication Security 4625 100121 User, logon type and failure code File integrity Wazuh FIM 550, 553, 554, 100130 Path, event kind, hashes where available SSH failures sshd / Wazuh 5763 Repetition, source IP and host identity Automated containment Ubuntu Active Response firewall-drop Action log, firewall rule and observed reachability Network policy pfSense logs Firewall/NAT policy Allowed HTTP vs. non-published service

Two separate measures are useful: detection correctness (a signal matches the intended behavior while the negative control does not) and response effectiveness (the requested temporary block is applied and then reverted). Latency analysis compares time-normalized timestamps for one identifiable event across the source and the SIEM; any reported rate or percentage requires an explicit sample size.

docs.title: 11.2. Engineering constraints
docs.text:
• IDS versus IPS: Suricata on pfSense is detection-only; Active Response blocks on the Ubuntu host, not at the network sensor.
  • Collection versus correlation: multiple sources appearing in Wazuh do not automatically create a joined incident timeline.
  • Signature uncertainty: a possible XXE signature describes a suspicious pattern, not a successful exploit.
  • FIM attribution: path/checksum changes do not establish which process initiated the change without additional auditing.
  • Authentication context: a single Windows 4625 event is a failed logon, not necessarily password spraying.
  • Source identity: SSH source IPs must be checked against NAT behavior before host-side blocking.
  • Tool compatibility: custom XML matches depend on the exact fields produced by the installed Wazuh and Sysmon versions.

docs.title: 11.3. Operational security
docs.text: The lab uses private VMnet networks and owned test systems. Firewall administration remains LAN-restricted, default administrative credentials must be replaced, configuration backups are sanitized and deliberately vulnerable services are kept isolated from the public Internet. Exported logs and screenshots are reviewed to avoid publication of credentials, tokens and private keys.

docs.title: 12. Conclusion
docs.text:
This project brings together network segmentation, a published vulnerable web application, Suricata signature detection and centralized host monitoring in a coherent SOC architecture. The documented network baseline shows real pfSense port forwarding and Suricata detections of Nmap NSE and potentially malicious HTTP patterns. The accompanying Wazuh configurations and analytical scenarios describe how network and endpoint signals are collected, classified, investigated and — for tightly scoped SSH failures — linked to temporary host containment.

The central engineering lesson is that a useful SOC alert must be attributable, explainable and verifiable. The documentation therefore distinguishes observed signature matches from confirmed compromise, detection from prevention, and a configured response from its measured effect.
